label: Review of Metric Spaces
notes: Appendix B is short but load-bearing: every later topological idea is first rehearsed here where distance makes the quantifiers concrete. Preview the arc from the three metric axioms through balls, open sets, convergence, continuity, completeness, and compactness, framing the metric as a training ground before topological abstraction takes over.

label: The Metric Axioms
notes: A metric keeps only the distance part of geometry, discarding vector addition, scalar multiplication, and coordinates. State positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality, and stress that these three conditions alone are strong enough to generate the entire local language of balls, open sets, limits, and continuity used throughout the book.

label: Four Metrics, Four Balls
notes: The unit ball changes shape with the metric even on a single fixed plane: round under the Euclidean norm, diamond under the taxicab norm, square under the sup metric, and a lone point under the discrete metric. This contrast is the cleanest motivation for abstracting topology away from any one distance formula.

label: The Triangle Inequality at Work
notes: The triangle inequality is the workhorse that makes open balls genuinely open. Trace the estimate for a point y inside a ball: any z near enough to y stays inside because its distance to the center is bounded by the detour through y. This single inequality powers openness, convergence, and continuity alike.

label: Open Sets and the Metric Topology
notes: Openness is a purely local containment test: every point of the set owns a ball that fits inside it. Arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets stay open, so the open balls generate a topology. This collection of open sets is exactly the structure topology later abstracts, discarding the metric itself.

label: Closed Sets and Sequence Limits
notes: A set is closed precisely when its complement is open, but in metric spaces a second reliable test exists: a closed set contains the limit of every convergent sequence drawn from it. This sequential characterization is the tool analysts and topologists reach for constantly when reasoning about limiting constructions and boundary behavior.

label: Convergence and Cauchy Tails
notes: Convergence names a destination, requiring every epsilon-ball about the limit to eventually swallow the tail. The Cauchy condition mentions no destination, asking only that the tail tightens in diameter. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy by the triangle inequality, but the converse can fail, which is the exact gap completeness closes.

label: Continuity: Two Equivalent Faces
notes: Metric continuity has a pointwise epsilon-delta form and a global open-preimage form, and they are the same radius argument read in opposite directions. Sketch how continuity converts target balls into domain balls, and how that conversion makes preimages of open sets open, building the central bridge from analysis into topology.

label: Uniform Continuity
notes: Uniform continuity strengthens ordinary continuity by demanding a single delta that works at every point for a given epsilon. Contrast pointwise continuity, where delta may shrink as the point moves, with the uniform version, and recall the theorem that continuous maps on compact metric spaces are automatically uniformly continuous.

label: Completeness
notes: A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence actually converges to a point inside it. Euclidean space is complete, while the open interval and the rationals are not, since they omit limits their own Cauchy data demand. Closed subsets of complete spaces inherit completeness, a fact used repeatedly in later chapters.

label: Compactness as Finite Control
notes: In metric spaces compactness fuses sequential compactness with total boundedness and completeness: every sequence has a convergent subsequence, and finite epsilon-nets cover the space at every scale. Closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space are the model examples, while the open interval leaks a limit and therefore fails to be compact.

label: Recap and Bridge to Topology
notes: Recap the dependency chain: axioms generate balls, balls generate open sets, open sets define convergence and continuity, and Cauchy behavior plus finite nets govern completeness and compactness. The next chapters keep the open-set behavior and discard the metric entirely, which is exactly the abstraction that point-set topology performs.
